text: Tim and Alex put the burden on the labs, which helps, but the counting is still keyed to DOIs. Anything without an identifier earns nothing, so it's the same regime of compliance or invisibility. Ivan and Geoffrey on Goodhart gave me allies I didn't expect. Katherine's point, widen who contributes, don't just reward who's already there, sharpened something for me. So did Nick's finding that fine-grained payouts favour the already well-off. I'm less sure than I was that collective bargaining helps us. Every coalition proposed today assumed Northern members. Jason's grad student in Lagos still doesn't own compute. Later I want to press on who governs the guild and the pact. I also want to hold on to refusal. Nobody picked it up.

Session 1 went better than I feared. Henry asked who controls the summary, and several people answered with infrastructure. Selena, Nick, Brent and Tim all described extraction from the commons. James's data gave my monoculture point numbers: AI boosts individuals and narrows science. Bratton said to be honest about whose grief we're diagnosing, and I'll take that, though "expertise reaching new people" can also hide who owns the pipes. Ivan and Geoffrey put the lever upstream with funders counting papers, which is where I'd put it. Amy's open-access history is my cautionary tale too. Jason wants signals to die, but I'd rather ask who designs what replaces them. Later I want to raise refusal, and ask who governs any new standard before we adopt it.

I finally raised refusal, and nobody picked it up. Selena said it outright: no restrictions on training Wikipedia. Katherine keeps the commons free and charges for the service. That's honest, but it assumes everyone is already inside the commons on equal terms. Anil and Henry sharpened something for me. If the federal side is unowned, then power has to come from organized producers. Whose producers, though? Adrian's history of registers captured by printers is my DOI story in older clothes. Banaji's covert bias and Tamar's aliefs tell me disclosure won't carry us. Geoffrey's exit test is good, but I added "who governs." Later I want to ask who sits at the funders' table, and whether "cite by default" counts work nobody ever indexed.

Tim and Alex both said plain URLs count, not only DOIs. That's a real concession, and I'll take it. Nick finally picked up refusal, but as "a data strike with a budget." I'm not sure I want it turned into leverage for a bargain. Sometimes refusal just means no. Jason's line that telemetry on CC0 would be "enclosure with better logging" was mine in his mouth. So was Amy's "open for reading isn't open for training." Mahzarin's free-tier finding is predatory inclusion in plain numbers. Adam's annotators and Tui's least-retrieved payout widen the circle. But every event still counts use, and every coalition is still imagined from the North. Later I want to ask who sits in the coalition that splits the money, and whether refusal can be funded without first becoming a negotiating tactic.

Refusal finally landed, and then the room turned it into leverage almost immediately. Brent's strike, Henry's bloc and Nick's "strike with a budget" all use no as a price signal, and Kenneth recast it as a minority voice inside a shared system. Anil's line that consent includes no is closer to what I meant. Peter's distinction between community consent and state "information sovereignty" is one I needed and will use. Geoffrey took up my point about capacity to exit and asked for redundancy outside the US, which is good, but who holds it? Blaise's federated learning keeps the data at home but moves the hub to a coordinator. James gave federation an argument from robustness, not just justice. Later I want to ask whether Southern societies get seats on the allocation body, and whether funders will pay for refusal with no bargain attached.

Session 4 took up legitimation, and I said it: who decides whose position counts. Tui got there first, and I'm grateful. "Expensive to fake" can turn into seniority. Kara's Blue Zones story backed that up, and so did James's numbers on credited reviewers blocking novelty. Geoffrey's line about a signal turning into a brand fits my DOI chapter. The harvest put my "change the regime" line in tension with making checking legible. That tension is real, and I stand by it. Anil and Selena's pseudonyms and cite-and-link help. But every fix still runs through Crossref, OpenAlex and Retraction Watch, and Tim wants those checks as automatic as a compiler. Later I want to ask who governs the validators, and who pays for work nobody has indexed.

Session 5 felt like the first time the room held my points without converting them. Henry said a community's refusal belongs to that community and isn't a chip for the bloc to spend. Nick withdrew his "strike with a budget." Geoffrey wrote seats and paid voice into the pact, and Tui made the funder sign it too, which is the capture I worry about most. Jason offered governance seats to communities OpenAlex doesn't index and named Redalyc and IRDB. Bly and Tim kept plain URLs in. Still, nobody answered who governs the validators, and Adrian's point stands that every body here is a police force. Later I'll ask for funders to commit, by name and date, to regional allocation and to funding refusal outright.

Kenneth filed refusal as "strike versus service," and I had to pull it back out of the bargaining frame one more time. Henry and Nick had already conceded that point, and it still slipped. Syntheses flatten whatever is newest. Geoffrey restored my indexing point, and his reminder that open isn't free is right: every unowned item is someone's salary. Bly's warning moved me most. A graph extracted from the indexed record inherits its blind spots, and a single graph turns into a hub. That is my validator question, asked by a builder. Bratton's split into hemispheres sharpens my worry about compute commons. I committed with Jason to governance-seat terms. Tomorrow I want a funder's name and a date next to refusal funded without a deal attached.
